newsitem.title: JAMAICA: FEATURE - Jamaica faces unusual forex dilemma.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Jamaica faces unusual forex dilemma.

text.p: Finance minister Omar Davies, having put Jamaica's twin tigers of rampant inflation and constant devaluation under control, now faces the unprecedented dilemma of having too much foreign exchange inflows.
The problem is a new one for Jamaica.
Since the currency began its freefall from J$1 to US$1.20 in the late 1960s, to J$40 to US$1 earlier this year, the scarcity of hard currency had begun to take on the appearance of permanence.

But data issued by the Bank of Jamaica shows that over the last four months, Davies has reined in growth in the money supply to the point where the local dollar revalued 12.5 pct, to J$35 to US$1 by the end of July.

In addition, inflation, which ran as high as 100 percent just four years ago, is now well within the one percent a month target, standing at 3.6 percent for the first four months of fiscal year 1996-97 (April-July), and net international reserves now stand at US$656.5 million, US$100 million above the end-of-fiscal-year target.

Total foreign exchange purchases between January and the end of August stood at US$1.18 billion, just shy of the total for 1995. Buoyed by strong remittance flows from overseas, the local currency has so far revalued another two percent in August, and Davies is confidently predicting that inflation for this month will come out at 0.5 percent.
The policy has not been without cost.

Jamaica's financial services sector, once the economic star performer, is now struggling for survival. Davies' tight monetary policies, which have pushed interest rates to above 40 percent, have already wiped out one bank, Century National, and pushed several others into the red.
But the finance minister observed that the continued strength in the foreign exchange market is proof that he is on the right course.

"If the tremors in the financial sector had happened one year ago," he told a meeting of customs brokers, "can you imagine what the reaction would have been...everybody would have rushed to convert to U.S. dollars."

Vivian Bedassie, market analyst for local stock brokers Edward Gayle & Co., noted: "There is certainly no reason to expect a devaluation in the short term and in fact a revaluation is far more likely."

Bedassie, like other analysts, believes local interest rates on government paper of as high as 40 percent earlier this year are attracting the strong inflow of overseas remittances. Overseas investors are apparently converting to local currency, putting the funds on deposit, and then reconverting to U.S. dollars after the interest is paid.
"That's the only thing that can account for it," he noted. "Inflows from tourism and other sectors aren't that much more than what they were last year."

The challenge to the government is how to restrain the strong revaluational pressures. So far, the government has done so by aggressively buying U.S. dollars, but cannot continue to do so without jeopardising the budget.

Analysts say Davies will either have to slash expenditure, let the dollar strengthen, or allow interest rates to fall faster than they have so far. The most recent Treasury bill offer saw rates falling nearly two percentage points, to 35.36 percent.
Based on recent historical data regarding drops in inflation and subsequent reductions in interest rates, many are predicting local rates could fall to 20 percent by year-end.
"As rates come down, government will have to watch what happens with the inflows," Bedassie stated. "As rates become less attractive, these flows could dry up."

On the other hand, the high interest rates have dried up lending and have squeezed the productive sector to the point of extinction. In the past, however, every attempt to lower interest rates has triggered a devaluation.

"I don't buy this argument about bringing down rates too quickly," noted Charles Ross, executive director of the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica. "The signal that the market is sending is that interest rates are too high."
He added that with substantial reserves on hand, "the government now how everything it needs to hold things together" should lower interest rates lead the Jamaican dollar to weaken.

"He (Davies) has got all kinds of problems," noted another investment executive who tracks the FE market for a local brokerage. "He's now faced with a situation where he has too many U.S. dollars and there are no Jamaican dollars in the system to buy them...he's gone overkill."
